drill.t: In ten years, we ___ with AI colleagues.
drill.vi: Mười năm nữa ta sẽ đang làm việc cùng đồng nghiệp AI.

drill.t: By the end of the year, they ___ the system.
drill.vi: Đến cuối năm, họ sẽ đã thử nghiệm xong hệ thống.

drill.t: At 9 p.m. tonight, I ___ my report.
drill.vi: Lúc 9 giờ tối nay tôi sẽ đang viết báo cáo.

lines.t: Which jobs are most at risk from AI?
lines.vi: Công việc nào có nguy cơ bị AI thay thế nhất?

lines.t: Probably jobs built around routine information processing, like basic data entry, simple translation or customer support scripts. Interestingly, it’s not necessarily low-paid jobs: plumbers and nurses seem much safer than some office roles, because their work is physical and unpredictable.
lines.vi: Có lẽ là công việc xoay quanh xử lý thông tin lặp lại, như nhập liệu cơ bản, dịch đơn giản hay chăm sóc khách hàng theo kịch bản. Thú vị là không hẳn việc lương thấp: thợ sửa ống nước và điều dưỡng có vẻ an toàn hơn nhiều so với một số vị trí văn phòng, vì công việc của họ mang tính thể chất và khó đoán.

lines.t: Should AI be allowed to make important decisions, for example in medicine?
lines.vi: Có nên để AI ra quyết định quan trọng, chẳng hạn trong y tế?

lines.t: As an assistant, certainly; as the final decision-maker, I’m much less comfortable. AI can arguably spot patterns in scans better than a tired doctor, but someone has to be accountable if it goes wrong, and you can’t really hold software responsible.
lines.vi: Làm trợ lý thì chắc chắn được; làm người ra quyết định cuối cùng thì tôi kém thoải mái hơn nhiều. AI có thể nói là phát hiện quy luật trên phim chụp tốt hơn bác sĩ mệt mỏi, nhưng phải có người chịu trách nhiệm nếu sai, mà bạn không thể bắt phần mềm chịu trách nhiệm.

lines.t: How should governments respond to AI?
lines.vi: Chính phủ nên ứng phó với AI thế nào?

lines.t: I’d say two things matter most: regulation that requires transparency about how important AI decisions are made, and serious investment in retraining. If people believe AI only benefits big companies, there will potentially be a strong backlash.
lines.vi: Tôi cho hai điều quan trọng nhất: quy định yêu cầu minh bạch về cách AI ra các quyết định quan trọng, và đầu tư nghiêm túc vào đào tạo lại. Nếu người dân tin rằng AI chỉ có lợi cho công ty lớn, có thể sẽ có phản ứng dữ dội.

gram2.title: Advanced hedging
gram2.rule: arguably · potentially · it is likely / unlikely that · there is a strong possibility that · to a large extent · it could be argued that
gram2.note: At band 7, hedging should be precise rather than vague. Arguably means “there are good reasons to say”. Potentially describes a risk that has not happened yet. It is likely that + clause sounds more academic than “maybe”. Combine hedging with evidence to sound both careful and confident.

ex.t: AI is arguably the most important technology of this century.
ex.vi: Có thể nói AI là công nghệ quan trọng nhất thế kỷ này.

ex.t: Facial recognition is potentially a threat to privacy.
ex.vi: Nhận diện khuôn mặt có khả năng đe doạ quyền riêng tư.

ex.t: It is likely that some jobs will disappear.
ex.vi: Nhiều khả năng một số công việc sẽ biến mất.

ex.t: It could be argued that AI increases inequality.
ex.vi: Có thể lập luận rằng AI làm tăng bất bình đẳng.

drill.t: This is ___ the biggest change since the internet.
drill.vi: Có thể nói đây là thay đổi lớn nhất kể từ internet.

drill.t: It is ___ that regulation will slow innovation.
drill.vi: Khó có khả năng quy định sẽ làm chậm đổi mới.

drill.t: The technology is ___ dangerous.
drill.vi: Công nghệ này có khả năng nguy hiểm.

drill.t: It could be ___ that AI helps students.
drill.vi: Có thể lập luận rằng AI giúp học sinh.

cue.card: Describe a time when technology did not work as you expected.
points: what you were trying to do
and explain how you felt about it
model: I’ll talk about the time I relied on a translation app during a business trip to Osaka last year. I was supposed to meet a supplier at a small workshop outside the city, and none of the staff there spoke English, so I assumed the app would handle everything.

For simple things it worked well — introductions, prices, delivery dates. But when we started discussing technical specifications, things went badly wrong. The app translated one of the supplier’s questions about “tolerance”, meaning the acceptable size difference for a component, as something about patience and tolerance between people. I gave a long, polite answer about our company values, and they looked completely confused.

At the time I felt embarrassed, and slightly annoyed with myself, because I’d prepared nothing else. In the end, the supplier’s daughter, who was studying engineering, arrived and helped us. Looking back, it taught me that these tools are incredibly useful for everyday situations, but potentially risky for specialised conversations. Now I always prepare a short glossary of key terms in advance — technology works best, I think, when it augments preparation rather than replaces it.

write.prompt: Artificial intelligence is now able to perform many tasks that were previously done by humans. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + answer (advantages outweigh, provided risks are managed)
Body 1: disadvantages — job displacement, bias, over-reliance; hiring example
Body 2: advantages — productivity, medical diagnosis, freeing people from routine work
Conclusion: answer again, with the conditions (transparency, retraining, human accountability)
model: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of carrying out work that once required human judgement, from writing reports to analysing medical scans. Although this development raises genuine concerns, I believe its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, provided that governments and companies manage the transition responsibly.

The drawbacks should not be underestimated. The most immediate is job displacement: roles built around routine information processing, such as data entry or basic customer service, are likely to shrink rapidly, and workers in their forties or fifties may find retraining difficult. A second problem is bias. Because AI systems learn from historical data, they can reproduce existing prejudices on a large scale, as shown by a recruitment tool that was abandoned after it was found to penalise female applicants. There is also a risk of over-reliance, whereby people gradually lose skills they no longer practise.

Nevertheless, the potential benefits are considerably greater. AI can dramatically increase productivity, allowing small businesses to complete in hours tasks that used to take days. In healthcare, systems that detect early signs of eye disease or cancer can help doctors in regions where specialists are scarce, potentially saving thousands of lives. Moreover, by automating repetitive work, AI can free employees to concentrate on tasks that require creativity, empathy and complex decision-making, which are arguably the most rewarding parts of most jobs.

In conclusion, while AI threatens some jobs and can amplify bias if poorly designed, its capacity to raise productivity and improve essential services such as healthcare makes it, on balance, a positive development. To ensure that these advantages are shared fairly, however, important decisions should remain subject to human accountability, and displaced workers must be given realistic opportunities to retrain.

lines.t: How many languages can you speak?

lines.t: Two well — Vietnamese and English — and I can get by in basic Japanese, mostly because of work. My Japanese is good enough for small talk, but definitely not for negotiations.
lines.vi: Hai thứ tiếng tốt — tiếng Việt và tiếng Anh — và tôi xoay xở được tiếng Nhật cơ bản, chủ yếu nhờ công việc. Tiếng Nhật của tôi đủ để nói chuyện xã giao, nhưng chắc chắn chưa đủ để đàm phán.

lines.t: What was the hardest part of learning English?

lines.t: Listening to native speakers in real life. Textbook recordings are slow and clear, so the first time I watched a film without subtitles, I understood almost nothing.
lines.vi: Nghe người bản xứ ngoài đời thực. Bài nghe trong sách chậm và rõ, nên lần đầu xem phim không phụ đề, tôi gần như không hiểu gì.

sents.t: When parents believe that a dominant language offers better opportunities, they often stop speaking their own language to their children.

sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, một số ngôn ngữ đã được hồi sinh thành công, như tiếng Wales ở Vương quốc Anh.

gram.title: Reporting verbs
gram.rule: argue / claim / suggest / point out / acknowledge / deny / warn + that … · recommend / encourage someone to … · accuse someone of …
gram.note: Reporting verbs show your attitude to a source. Claim suggests doubt; point out and acknowledge suggest the point is true; argue is neutral. Using a range of them improves Lexical Resource and helps you present opinions you don’t share: Critics claim that … However, research suggests that … Watch the patterns: suggest + that/-ing, encourage + someone + to.

dlg2.title: Part 3: languages in the modern world

lines.t: Is it important for everyone to learn English?
lines.vi: Có cần thiết mọi người đều học tiếng Anh không?

lines.t: For anyone who wants to work internationally or study at a high level, it’s almost essential, since so much research and business happens in English. But I wouldn’t say everyone needs it; a farmer in a rural area may benefit far more from other skills.
lines.vi: Với ai muốn làm việc quốc tế hay học ở trình độ cao thì gần như thiết yếu, vì rất nhiều nghiên cứu và kinh doanh diễn ra bằng tiếng Anh. Nhưng tôi không nói ai cũng cần; một nông dân ở vùng nông thôn có thể được lợi nhiều hơn từ kỹ năng khác.

lines.t: Does it matter if small languages die out?
lines.vi: Ngôn ngữ nhỏ biến mất có quan trọng không?

lines.t: I think it does. A language isn’t just a set of words; it contains a community’s knowledge, its stories and its way of seeing the world. When it disappears, that knowledge is often lost too, for example detailed names for local plants and their medical uses.
lines.vi: Tôi nghĩ có. Ngôn ngữ không chỉ là tập hợp từ ngữ; nó chứa tri thức, câu chuyện và cách nhìn thế giới của cộng đồng. Khi nó biến mất, tri thức đó thường mất theo, ví dụ tên gọi chi tiết các loài cây địa phương và công dụng chữa bệnh của chúng.

lines.t: Will translation technology make language learning unnecessary?
lines.vi: Công nghệ dịch có khiến việc học ngoại ngữ trở nên không cần thiết?

lines.t: For practical tasks like reading a menu, perhaps. But you can’t build a real friendship or understand humour through an app. Learning a language also changes how you think, so I suspect it will become less necessary but no less valuable.
lines.vi: Với việc thực tế như đọc thực đơn thì có lẽ. Nhưng bạn không thể xây dựng tình bạn thật hay hiểu sự hài hước qua một ứng dụng. Học ngôn ngữ còn thay đổi cách bạn suy nghĩ, nên tôi đoán nó sẽ ít cần thiết hơn nhưng không kém giá trị.

gram2.title: Articles with general and abstract nouns
gram2.rule: zero article for general ideas (Language reflects culture) · the for specific ones (the language of my grandparents) · a/an for one example (a language with 50 speakers)
gram2.note: Article errors are very common even at band 7. Use no article when you mean something in general: Education is important. Technology changes quickly. Use the when the noun is made specific by context or a phrase after it: the education I received, the technology used in schools. Uncountable nouns never take a/an.

cue.card: Describe a time when you had difficulty communicating with someone.
points: and explain how you solved the problem
model: I’d like to describe a conversation I had with an elderly man in a village in Ha Giang province, near the Chinese border, when I was trekking there a couple of years ago.

I’d got separated from my group and was trying to find the homestay where we were supposed to spend the night. The man I asked was Hmong and spoke very little Vietnamese, and of course I don’t speak any Hmong at all. To make things worse, my phone had no signal, so I couldn’t show him a map or use a translation app.

In the end we solved it in a very old-fashioned way. I said the name of the homestay owner several times and drew a rough picture of a house with a flag, which was the homestay’s sign. He laughed, pointed at the picture, and then simply walked with me for twenty minutes until we got there. What struck me afterwards was how much we managed to communicate without any shared language — through gestures, tone of voice and patience. It also made me realise, slightly uncomfortably, that I’d assumed everyone in my own country speaks Vietnamese, which simply isn’t true.

write.prompt: Some people think that children should learn a foreign language from primary school, while others believe it is better to start at secondary school. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views + position (primary, if teaching quality is good)
Body 1: arguments for secondary — mother tongue first, curriculum pressure, lack of qualified teachers
Body 2: arguments for primary — pronunciation, confidence, more total hours; research
Conclusion: position + condition
model: Opinions differ on the ideal age for children to begin learning a foreign language at school. While some argue that it is better to wait until secondary school, others believe that primary school is the right starting point. In my view, an early start is preferable, but only if lessons are taught by well-trained teachers.

Those who favour a later start make several reasonable points. Young children are still developing literacy in their mother tongue, and some educators claim that introducing a second language too early may slow this process. In addition, the primary curriculum is already crowded, so time spent on a foreign language may be taken from subjects such as mathematics or reading. Perhaps the strongest argument is a practical one: in many countries there are not enough qualified primary teachers, and a weak teacher can give children poor pronunciation and a lasting dislike of the subject.

On the other hand, there are clear advantages to starting earlier. Children who begin before the age of ten generally find it easier to acquire native-like pronunciation, and they tend to be less anxious about making mistakes, which helps them become confident speakers. Moreover, an early start simply gives learners more total hours of exposure before they leave school, and research consistently shows that the number of hours is one of the strongest predictors of eventual proficiency. Learning a second language may also have cognitive benefits, such as improved concentration.

In conclusion, although concerns about the curriculum and teacher quality are valid, I believe the benefits of beginning a foreign language at primary school outweigh the drawbacks. The priority for governments should therefore be to train enough specialist teachers, so that children receive high-quality teaching from the start.

lines.t: What do you like most about your home?

lines.t: The balcony, without a doubt. It’s tiny, but it gets the morning sun and a breeze in the evening, which matters a lot in a city as hot and densely populated as mine.
lines.vi: Ban công, chắc chắn. Nó nhỏ xíu nhưng có nắng sáng và gió chiều, điều rất quan trọng ở một thành phố nóng và đông dân như chỗ tôi.

lines.t: Do you rent or own your home?
lines.vi: Bạn thuê hay sở hữu nhà?

lines.t: I rent at the moment. Buying would mean a huge mortgage, and to be honest I like the flexibility, although I don’t enjoy having to ask the landlord every time something breaks.
lines.vi: Hiện tôi thuê. Mua nhà đồng nghĩa với khoản vay rất lớn, và thật lòng tôi thích sự linh hoạt, dù không thích lần nào hỏng gì cũng phải hỏi chủ nhà.

lines.t: Would you change anything about it?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn thay đổi gì không?

lines.t: Better soundproofing. The walls are so thin that I know exactly which TV series my neighbours are watching.
lines.vi: Cách âm tốt hơn. Tường mỏng đến mức tôi biết chính xác hàng xóm đang xem phim gì.

sents.t: Around half of Vienna’s residents live in social housing owned or subsidised by the city.
sents.vi: Khoảng một nửa cư dân Vienna sống trong nhà ở xã hội do thành phố sở hữu hoặc trợ cấp.

sents.t: Unlike in many countries, these homes are not only for the poor; middle-income families are also eligible.
sents.vi: Khác với nhiều nước, những căn nhà này không chỉ dành cho người nghèo; gia đình thu nhập trung bình cũng đủ điều kiện.

sents.t: Because the city is such a large landlord, it can keep rents stable across the whole market.
sents.vi: Vì thành phố là chủ nhà lớn như vậy, họ có thể giữ giá thuê ổn định trên toàn thị trường.

sents.t: As a result, Viennese households typically spend a smaller share of their income on housing than people in London or Paris.
sents.vi: Kết quả là các hộ ở Vienna thường chi tỉ lệ thu nhập cho nhà ở thấp hơn người ở London hay Paris.

sents.t: Critics note, however, that waiting lists can be long and that the model took a century to build.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, những người phê bình lưu ý danh sách chờ có thể dài và mô hình này mất cả thế kỷ để xây dựng.

q.q: Social housing in Vienna is available only to low-income families.
The model has taken around a hundred years to develop.
Vienna’s social housing is cheaper to build than private housing.

gram.title: The more …, the more …
gram.rule: the + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause · The higher prices rise, the fewer people can afford … · the sooner, the better
gram.note: This structure shows that two changes are linked. Both halves start with the + comparative, and each half needs its own clause (usually subject + verb). It is excellent for explaining cause and effect in Part 3 and Task 2: The more cities grow, the more important public transport becomes.

ex.t: The bigger a city becomes, the more expensive housing gets.
ex.vi: Thành phố càng lớn, nhà càng đắt.

ex.t: The longer you rent, the less you save for a deposit.

lines.t: Why is housing so expensive in big cities?
lines.vi: Vì sao nhà ở thành phố lớn đắt đến vậy?

lines.t: It’s mainly supply and demand. The more jobs a city offers, the more people move there, but land is limited and building takes years. On top of that, many apartments are bought as investments and left vacant, which reduces the supply even further.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu là cung và cầu. Thành phố càng nhiều việc làm thì càng nhiều người chuyển đến, nhưng đất có hạn và xây dựng mất nhiều năm. Thêm vào đó, nhiều căn hộ được mua để đầu tư rồi bỏ trống, khiến nguồn cung càng giảm.

lines.t: Is it important to own your own home?
lines.vi: Sở hữu nhà riêng có quan trọng không?

lines.t: Culturally, it’s very important in Vietnam — owning a house is seen as a sign of stability. Personally, I think secure, affordable renting can work just as well, as it does in Germany, but only if tenants have proper legal protection.
lines.vi: Về văn hoá thì rất quan trọng ở Việt Nam — có nhà được coi là dấu hiệu ổn định. Cá nhân tôi nghĩ thuê nhà ổn định, giá phải chăng cũng tốt như vậy, như ở Đức, nhưng chỉ khi người thuê được pháp luật bảo vệ đầy đủ.

lines.t: Should new buildings look modern or traditional?
lines.vi: Nhà mới nên trông hiện đại hay truyền thống?

lines.t: I don’t think it has to be either. The best new buildings I’ve seen use modern materials but borrow traditional ideas, like deep roofs for shade and courtyards for ventilation, so they blend in while still being functional.
lines.vi: Tôi không nghĩ phải chọn một. Những công trình mới hay nhất tôi từng thấy dùng vật liệu hiện đại nhưng mượn ý tưởng truyền thống, như mái sâu để che nắng và sân trong để thông gió, nên chúng vừa hoà hợp vừa tiện dụng.

gram2.title: Passive reporting structures
gram2.rule: It is said / believed / estimated that … · Subject + is said / thought / reported + to + verb (to be, to have + past participle)
gram2.note: These structures report common opinions or data without naming a source, which is useful in essays. Two patterns are possible: It is estimated that prices have doubled. / Prices are estimated to have doubled. Use to have + past participle for something that happened earlier than the reporting.

ex.t: It is estimated that 30% of homes are empty.

cue.card: Describe a building you find beautiful or interesting.
points: and explain why you find it beautiful or interesting
model: I’d like to describe the Hanoi Opera House, which stands at the end of Trang Tien Street, right in the French quarter. It was completed in 1911 and is said to have been modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris, though it’s much smaller.

It’s a pale yellow building with white columns, tall arched windows and a grey slate roof, and there’s a wide flight of steps leading up to the main entrance. At night it’s lit up from below, which makes it look almost golden. Inside, it’s still used for what it was built for — opera, classical concerts and ballet — and it also hosts official ceremonies.

What I find interesting is its history rather than just its appearance. It was built by the colonial government as a symbol of French culture, yet in 1945 the square in front of it was where huge crowds gathered during the August Revolution. So the same building represents two completely different chapters of the country’s past. I also think it shows that the more carefully a building is maintained, the more it becomes part of a city’s identity, even if its origins are complicated.

write.prompt: The line graph shows average house prices and average annual household income in one city between 2000 and 2025 (in thousands of dollars). Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both lines
Overview: both rose, but prices rose far faster, so the gap (ratio) widened dramatically
Body 1: house prices — period of fastest growth (2005–2010, 2015–2020), figures
Body 2: income — slow steady rise; calculate the ratio 4 → about 8.5
model: The line graph compares the average price of a house with the average annual income of households in a particular city over a 25-year period from 2000 to 2025.
Overall, both figures increased, but house prices grew far more rapidly than incomes. Consequently, homes became considerably less affordable for the typical household over the period.

In 2000, the average house cost $60,000. Prices then climbed steadily to $85,000 in 2005 before rising sharply to $140,000 by 2010. After a period of slower growth, they surged again between 2015 and 2020, reaching $240,000, and by 2025 they stood at $290,000, almost five times the original level.

Household income, by contrast, rose slowly but consistently throughout the period, from $15,000 to $34,000, an increase of just over 120%. As a result, while an average house cost four times the annual household income in 2000, by 2025 it was worth roughly eight and a half years of earnings.

units.title: News, media & trust
units.goal: Discuss news sources, misinformation and media influence, using quantifiers and cohesive reference.

words.ex: Trust in mainstream media has declined.
words.exVi: Niềm tin vào truyền thông chính thống đã giảm.

words.ex: Check whether the source is credible.
words.exVi: Kiểm tra xem nguồn có đáng tin không.

words.ex: Sensationalism attracts clicks but damages trust.
words.exVi: Giật gân thu hút lượt nhấp nhưng làm mất niềm tin.

words.ex: The headline was pure clickbait.
words.exVi: Tiêu đề hoàn toàn là câu nhấp chuột.

words.ex: Journalists must fact-check every claim.
words.exVi: Nhà báo phải kiểm chứng mọi khẳng định.

words.vi: buồng vang (chỉ nghe ý kiến giống mình)
words.ex: Social media can create echo chambers.
words.exVi: Mạng xã hội có thể tạo ra buồng vang.

words.ex: Censorship limits what citizens can learn.
words.exVi: Kiểm duyệt hạn chế điều công dân được biết.

words.ex: Press freedom is essential in a democracy.
words.exVi: Tự do báo chí là thiết yếu trong một nền dân chủ.

words.ex: Investigative journalism exposed the scandal.
words.exVi: Báo chí điều tra đã phanh phui vụ bê bối.

words.ex: The report was clearly biased.
words.exVi: Bài báo rõ ràng thiên vị.

words.ex: News should be objective.
words.exVi: Tin tức nên khách quan.

words.ex: The video went viral overnight.

words.ex: False rumours circulated on messaging apps.
words.exVi: Tin đồn sai lan truyền trên ứng dụng nhắn tin.

words.ex: Tabloids focus on celebrity gossip.
words.exVi: Báo lá cải tập trung vào chuyện phiếm người nổi tiếng.

words.ex: The election received huge coverage.
words.exVi: Cuộc bầu cử được đưa tin rầm rộ.

words.ex: The media can shape public opinion.
words.exVi: Truyền thông có thể định hướng dư luận.

words.vi: năng lực hiểu biết truyền thông
words.ex: Schools should teach media literacy.
words.exVi: Trường học nên dạy năng lực hiểu biết truyền thông.

words.vi: tường phí (phải trả tiền để đọc)
words.ex: Quality newspapers often use a paywall.
words.exVi: Báo chất lượng thường đặt tường phí.

words.ex: The article distorted the minister’s words.
words.exVi: Bài báo bóp méo lời bộ trưởng.

words.ex: Politicians should be under public scrutiny.
words.exVi: Chính trị gia nên chịu sự giám sát của công chúng.

lines.t: How do you usually get the news?
lines.vi: Bạn thường cập nhật tin tức bằng cách nào?

lines.t: Mostly through a news app in the morning, plus whatever appears on social media during the day. I try not to rely on the second one, because a lot of what circulates there hasn’t been fact-checked.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu qua một ứng dụng tin tức buổi sáng, cộng với những gì hiện lên trên mạng xã hội trong ngày. Tôi cố không dựa vào cái thứ hai, vì nhiều thứ lan truyền ở đó chưa được kiểm chứng.

lines.t: What kind of news interests you most?
lines.vi: Loại tin nào bạn quan tâm nhất?

lines.t: Science and business, generally. I tend to skip celebrity news; I find most of it pretty trivial.
lines.vi: Nhìn chung là khoa học và kinh doanh. Tôi thường bỏ qua tin người nổi tiếng; tôi thấy phần lớn khá vụn vặt.

lines.t: Do you trust the news you read?
lines.vi: Bạn có tin những tin tức mình đọc không?

lines.t: It depends on the source. I trust established outlets more, but even then I compare two or three before I believe anything important.
lines.vi: Còn tuỳ nguồn. Tôi tin các cơ quan báo chí lâu năm hơn, nhưng kể cả vậy tôi vẫn so sánh hai ba nguồn trước khi tin điều gì quan trọng.

sents.t: A 2018 study of millions of posts found that false news stories spread significantly faster than true ones.
sents.vi: Một nghiên cứu năm 2018 trên hàng triệu bài đăng cho thấy tin giả lan nhanh hơn đáng kể so với tin thật.

sents.t: The researchers had expected automated accounts to be responsible, but most of the sharing was done by real people.
sents.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu từng nghĩ tài khoản tự động là thủ phạm, nhưng phần lớn việc chia sẻ do người thật thực hiện.

sents.t: False stories tended to be more surprising and to provoke stronger emotions, such as fear or disgust.
sents.vi: Tin giả thường gây bất ngờ hơn và khơi dậy cảm xúc mạnh hơn như sợ hãi hay ghê tởm.

sents.t: This suggests that the problem lies partly in human psychology rather than only in technology.
sents.vi: Điều này cho thấy vấn đề nằm một phần ở tâm lý con người chứ không chỉ ở công nghệ.

sents.t: Some platforms now ask users whether they have read an article before allowing them to share it.
sents.vi: Một số nền tảng giờ hỏi người dùng đã đọc bài chưa trước khi cho chia sẻ.

q.q: Automated accounts were the main cause of false news spreading.
False stories often caused stronger emotional reactions.
Asking users to read before sharing has halved misinformation.

gram.title: Quantifiers for precise claims
gram.rule: a great deal of / little / a little (uncountable) · many / few / a few (countable) · a significant number of · the vast majority of · hardly any
gram.note: Precise quantifiers avoid over-generalising (“all people”, “everyone”). Remember: few and little are negative (almost none), a few and a little are positive (some). A great deal of goes with uncountable nouns; a large number of with countable nouns. The majority of + plural noun takes a plural verb.

ex.t: A great deal of misinformation spreads through private groups.
ex.vi: Rất nhiều thông tin sai lan qua các nhóm kín.

ex.t: Few young people buy printed newspapers.
ex.vi: Rất ít người trẻ mua báo giấy.

ex.t: A significant number of readers never check sources.
ex.vi: Một số lượng đáng kể độc giả không bao giờ kiểm tra nguồn.

ex.t: The vast majority of viral stories are never corrected.
ex.vi: Đại đa số câu chuyện lan truyền không bao giờ được đính chính.

drill.t: ___ people read the whole article.
drill.vi: Rất ít người đọc toàn bộ bài báo.

drill.t: There is ___ evidence for this claim.
drill.vi: Có rất ít bằng chứng cho khẳng định này.

drill.t: A great deal of ___ is shared online.
drill.vi: Rất nhiều thông tin được chia sẻ trên mạng.

drill.t: The majority of users ___ on their phones.
drill.vi: Phần lớn người dùng đọc tin trên điện thoại.

lines.t: Is social media a good source of news?
lines.vi: Mạng xã hội có phải nguồn tin tốt không?

lines.t: It’s fast, and occasionally it reports events before traditional media can get there. But it rewards whatever gets attention, so sensationalism and clickbait do well. And because algorithms show you what you already agree with, it can trap people in echo chambers.
lines.vi: Nó nhanh, và đôi khi đưa tin sự kiện trước cả truyền thông truyền thống. Nhưng nó thưởng cho thứ thu hút sự chú ý, nên giật gân và câu nhấp chuột lên ngôi. Và vì thuật toán cho bạn thấy điều bạn vốn đồng ý, nó có thể nhốt người ta trong buồng vang.

lines.t: Should governments control the media?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có nên kiểm soát truyền thông?

lines.t: Control, no — that leads to censorship, and the media’s job is partly to keep governments under scrutiny. Regulation is different, though. Rules about hate speech or protecting children’s privacy seem perfectly reasonable.
lines.vi: Kiểm soát thì không — điều đó dẫn đến kiểm duyệt, mà nhiệm vụ của truyền thông một phần là giám sát chính phủ. Tuy nhiên điều tiết thì khác. Quy định về ngôn từ thù ghét hay bảo vệ quyền riêng tư của trẻ em có vẻ hoàn toàn hợp lý.

lines.t: Will newspapers disappear?
lines.vi: Báo in có biến mất không?

lines.t: Printed ones, mostly, yes. But quality journalism will survive if people pay for it. The worrying part is that this creates a two-tier system: those who can afford paywalls get reliable news, while others get whatever is free.
lines.vi: Báo giấy thì phần lớn có. Nhưng báo chí chất lượng sẽ tồn tại nếu người ta trả tiền. Điều đáng lo là nó tạo ra hệ thống hai tầng: ai trả được tường phí thì có tin đáng tin, còn người khác nhận bất cứ thứ gì miễn phí.

gram2.title: Cohesion with reference words
gram2.rule: this / these + noun (this trend, these problems) · the former / the latter · such + noun · which refers to the whole idea
gram2.note: Coherence and Cohesion is 25% of your Writing score. Instead of repeating nouns, refer back with this + a summary noun: Many people now get news from social media. This shift has … The former and the latter refer to the first and second of two things just mentioned. Avoid starting a sentence with “It” or “This” alone when the reference is unclear.

ex.t: Fewer people buy newspapers. This decline has hit local journalism hardest.

cue.card: Describe a news story that interested you.
points: and explain why it interested you
model: The story I’d like to talk about was the rescue of a youth football team from a flooded cave in northern Thailand in 2018. I first saw it as a short headline on my phone, but over the next two weeks I followed it almost hourly, like millions of people around the world.

Twelve boys and their coach had gone into the cave after practice and were trapped when heavy rain flooded the passages. Divers took nine days just to find them, sitting on a rock ledge in the dark, and then there was a huge debate about how to get them out, because none of the boys could dive. Eventually an international team of cave divers guided them out one by one, partly sedated, over three days. Sadly, one former Thai navy diver died during the operation.

The reaction was extraordinary — people of every nationality were sharing updates and praying for them. What interested me was partly the sheer human drama, but also the coverage itself. Some outlets were careful and accurate, while others spread wild rumours that went viral. It was the first time I consciously noticed the difference between credible reporting and sensationalism, and since then I’ve been much more careful about where I get my news.

write.prompt: Many people now get their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. Is this a positive or negative development?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + position (largely negative unless media literacy improves)
Body 1: positives — speed, access, diverse voices, citizen journalism
Body 2: negatives — misinformation spreads faster, echo chambers, collapse of funding for investigative journalism
Conclusion: position + what would make it positive
model: A growing proportion of people now rely on social media platforms for news instead of traditional newspapers and broadcasters. Although this shift has made information faster and more accessible, I believe it is, on balance, a negative development, mainly because it has made misinformation easier to spread and weakened professional journalism.

There are undeniable benefits. Social media allows news to travel in seconds, and during natural disasters it can provide life-saving updates long before television can broadcast them. It has also given a voice to people who were previously ignored by the mainstream media; ordinary citizens with a smartphone can now document events, from police misconduct to environmental damage, that might otherwise never have been reported. In addition, much of this content is free, which matters in countries where newspapers are expensive.

However, these advantages are outweighed by serious problems. Research has shown that false stories spread considerably faster than accurate ones on social platforms, because they tend to be more surprising and emotionally charged. Moreover, algorithms that show users content similar to what they have already engaged with can create echo chambers, reinforcing existing beliefs and deepening political divisions. Perhaps most damaging in the long term is the impact on funding: as advertising revenue has moved to technology companies, many newspapers have been forced to cut investigative teams, which are expensive but essential for holding the powerful to account.

In conclusion, while social media has made news more immediate and has broadened the range of voices heard, its tendency to amplify misinformation and undermine quality journalism makes this trend largely negative. It could become more positive, however, if schools taught media literacy and platforms took greater responsibility for the accuracy of what they promote.

units.title: Wildlife & biodiversity

lines.t: Do you like animals?
lines.vi: Bạn có thích động vật không?

lines.t: Very much, though I’ve never been able to keep a pet because my apartment is too small. I make up for it by watching far too many wildlife documentaries.
lines.vi: Rất thích, dù tôi chưa bao giờ nuôi được thú cưng vì căn hộ quá nhỏ. Tôi bù lại bằng cách xem quá nhiều phim tài liệu về động vật hoang dã.

lines.t: Have you ever seen wild animals in nature?
lines.vi: Bạn đã bao giờ thấy động vật hoang dã ngoài tự nhiên chưa?

lines.t: A few times. The most memorable was seeing a family of langurs in Cuc Phuong National Park. We had to stay completely still so as not to frighten them.
lines.vi: Vài lần. Đáng nhớ nhất là thấy một gia đình voọc ở Vườn quốc gia Cúc Phương. Chúng tôi phải đứng im hoàn toàn để không làm chúng sợ.

lines.t: Do you think zoos are a good idea?
lines.vi: Bạn nghĩ sở thú có phải ý hay không?

lines.t: Good ones, yes, the kind that focus on conservation and breeding endangered species. But small zoos where animals live in tiny cages are hard to justify.
lines.vi: Sở thú tốt thì có, loại tập trung vào bảo tồn và nhân giống loài nguy cấp. Nhưng sở thú nhỏ nơi thú sống trong lồng chật hẹp thì khó biện minh.

sents.t: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, seventy years after they had been hunted to local extinction.
sents.vi: Sói được tái thả vào Vườn quốc gia Yellowstone năm 1995, bảy mươi năm sau khi bị săn đến tuyệt chủng tại chỗ.

sents.t: Without predators, the deer population had grown so large that it had eaten most young trees along the rivers.
sents.vi: Không có thú săn mồi, quần thể hươu đã tăng lớn đến mức ăn gần hết cây non dọc sông.

sents.t: Once the wolves returned, the deer avoided open river valleys, and the trees began to recover.
sents.vi: Khi sói trở lại, hươu tránh các thung lũng sông trống trải, và cây cối bắt đầu hồi phục.

sents.t: The returning trees provided food and shelter for birds and beavers.
sents.vi: Cây cối hồi sinh cung cấp thức ăn và nơi trú cho chim và hải ly.

sents.t: Some ecologists now argue that the effects have been exaggerated, but most agree that the wolves had a significant impact on the ecosystem.
sents.vi: Một số nhà sinh thái học giờ cho rằng tác động đã bị phóng đại, nhưng phần lớn đồng ý sói đã ảnh hưởng đáng kể đến hệ sinh thái.

q.q: Wolves had been absent from Yellowstone for about seventy years before 1995.
All ecologists agree about the size of the wolves’ effect.
The number of wolves in Yellowstone has doubled since 2010.

gram.title: Mixed conditionals
gram.rule: If + past perfect, would + verb (past cause → present result) · If + past simple, would have + past participle (present situation → past result)
gram.note: Mixed conditionals connect different times. The most common type describes how a past event affects the present: If the forest had not been cut down, the area would still have tigers today. These are very useful for discussing environmental damage and history in Part 3.

ex.t: If wolves had not been reintroduced, the rivers would look very different today.
ex.vi: Nếu sói không được tái thả, các con sông hôm nay sẽ trông rất khác.

ex.t: If we had protected the forests earlier, more species would survive now.
ex.vi: Nếu ta bảo vệ rừng sớm hơn, giờ sẽ có nhiều loài sống sót hơn.

ex.t: If people cared more about nature, they would have stopped this long ago.
ex.vi: Nếu người ta quan tâm thiên nhiên hơn, họ đã ngăn chuyện này từ lâu.

ex.t: If the law had been enforced, rhinos would still live in Vietnam.
ex.vi: Nếu luật được thực thi, tê giác vẫn còn sống ở Việt Nam.

drill.t: If they had banned hunting, there ___ more birds now.
drill.vi: Nếu họ cấm săn bắt, giờ đã có nhiều chim hơn.

drill.t: If the dam ___ built, the river would still have fish.
drill.vi: Nếu con đập không được xây, sông vẫn còn cá.

drill.vi: Nếu cô ấy dũng cảm hơn, cô ấy đã nhận công việc ở châu Phi.

drill.vi: Hôm nay ta đã có không khí sạch nếu ngừng dùng than sớm hơn.

lines.t: Why should we protect animals that are not useful to humans?
lines.vi: Vì sao phải bảo vệ những loài không có ích cho con người?

lines.t: First, “useful” is hard to judge — we often don’t know a species’ role until it’s gone, as the wolves in Yellowstone showed. Ecosystems are interconnected, so losing one species can affect pollination, water quality or pest control. And second, many people would argue we simply have a moral responsibility not to destroy other forms of life.
lines.vi: Thứ nhất, “có ích” rất khó đánh giá — ta thường không biết vai trò của một loài cho đến khi nó mất đi, như sói ở Yellowstone đã cho thấy. Hệ sinh thái liên kết với nhau, nên mất một loài có thể ảnh hưởng thụ phấn, chất lượng nước hay kiểm soát sâu bệnh. Thứ hai, nhiều người cho rằng đơn giản là ta có trách nhiệm đạo đức không huỷ diệt các dạng sống khác.

lines.t: Is it fair to ask poor communities to protect wildlife?
lines.vi: Có công bằng khi yêu cầu cộng đồng nghèo bảo vệ động vật hoang dã?

lines.t: Only if they benefit. If an elephant destroys a family’s harvest, it’s unrealistic to expect them to love elephants. Programmes that share tourism income with villages, or pay people to work as rangers, have been far more successful than simply banning things.
lines.vi: Chỉ khi họ được lợi. Nếu voi phá mùa màng của một gia đình, mong họ yêu voi là phi thực tế. Các chương trình chia sẻ thu nhập du lịch với làng, hay trả tiền cho người dân làm kiểm lâm, thành công hơn nhiều so với chỉ ra lệnh cấm.

lines.t: Can technology help conservation?
lines.vi: Công nghệ có giúp bảo tồn không?

lines.t: Definitely. Drones and camera traps help count animals in remote areas, and DNA testing can identify where illegal ivory comes from. But technology can’t replace political will — the tools are useless if laws aren’t enforced.
lines.vi: Chắc chắn. Drone và bẫy ảnh giúp đếm động vật ở vùng xa xôi, và xét nghiệm ADN có thể xác định ngà voi lậu từ đâu. Nhưng công nghệ không thay được ý chí chính trị — công cụ vô dụng nếu luật không được thực thi.

gram2.title: Expressing purpose
gram2.rule: to / in order to / so as to + verb · in order not to / so as not to · so that + subject + can / could / will · with the aim of + -ing
gram2.note: Purpose clauses explain why an action is taken, which is essential when you propose solutions in Task 2. Use so that when the subject changes: Parks were created so that animals could move safely. For negative purpose, use so as not to or in order not to (not “to not”).

ex.t: Rangers patrol at night in order to stop poachers.
ex.vi: Kiểm lâm tuần tra ban đêm để ngăn săn trộm.

ex.t: Bridges were built so that animals could cross the highway.
ex.vi: Cầu được xây để động vật có thể băng qua cao tốc.

ex.t: Tourists keep their distance so as not to disturb the birds.
ex.vi: Du khách giữ khoảng cách để không làm phiền chim.

ex.t: The law was passed with the aim of reducing the ivory trade.
ex.vi: Luật được thông qua nhằm giảm buôn bán ngà voi.

drill.vi: Họ rào cánh đồng để voi không vào được.

drill.t: Walk quietly so as ___ the animals.
drill.vi: Đi nhẹ nhàng để không làm thú sợ.

drill.t: The reserve was created in order ___ the forest.
drill.vi: Khu bảo tồn được lập để bảo vệ rừng.

drill.t: The project began with the aim of ___ tigers.
drill.vi: Dự án bắt đầu với mục tiêu cứu loài hổ.

cue.card: Describe a natural place you visited that you enjoyed.
points: and explain why you enjoyed it
model: I’d like to talk about Cat Tien National Park, about four hours north of Ho Chi Minh City. I went there with my brother during the dry season last year, mainly because we’d read that it’s one of the last areas of lowland forest left in southern Vietnam.

We stayed two nights in a basic guesthouse inside the park. During the day we cycled along forest trails and visited a primate rescue centre, where gibbons that had been taken from the illegal wildlife trade are rehabilitated so that they can eventually be released. On the second evening we went on a night safari in an open truck and saw deer, a civet and, very briefly, a slow loris, which was the highlight for me.

I enjoyed it for two reasons. First, the sheer scale of the trees made me feel genuinely small, in a good way, after months of city life. Second, talking to the rangers changed my understanding of conservation. They explained that if the park hadn’t been protected in the 1990s, most of this forest would be coffee plantations today. It made me realise how fragile these places are, and how much they depend on decisions made by just a few people.

write.prompt: The diagram below shows the life cycle of the salmon, a type of fish. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
write.data: Stage 1 (upper river, slow-moving water, among small stones): eggs laid, hatch in 5–6 months → Stage 2 (lower river, fast-moving water, among reeds): young fish (“fry”, 3–8 cm) live here for about 4 years → Stage 3: “smolt” (12–15 cm) migrate downstream to the sea → Stage 4 (open sea): adult salmon (70–76 cm) spend about 5 years → Stage 5: adults swim back upriver to the upper river to lay eggs; cycle repeats.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (life cycle → stages in the life of)
Overview: cyclical, freshwater → sea → freshwater; about ten years; size increases greatly
Body 1: river stages — eggs, fry, smolt; locations and sizes
Body 2: sea stage and return journey
model: The diagram illustrates the various stages in the life of the salmon, from eggs in a river to adult fish in the open sea.

Overall, the salmon’s life is a cycle that begins and ends in the upper part of a river, with a long period spent at sea in between. The whole process lasts around ten years, during which the fish grows from a tiny egg to an adult of over 70 centimetres.

The cycle starts when salmon eggs are laid among small stones in the slow-moving water of the upper river, where they hatch after five to six months. The young fish, known as fry and measuring between 3 and 8 centimetres, then move to the faster-flowing lower river, where they shelter among reeds for approximately four years. Having grown to 12–15 centimetres, they become smolt and begin migrating downstream towards the sea.

Once they reach the open sea, the salmon spend about five years there, growing into adults of between 70 and 76 centimetres. Finally, the mature fish swim all the way back up the river to the area where they were born in order to lay their own eggs, and the cycle begins again.

lines.t: What did you enjoy doing as a child?
lines.vi: Hồi nhỏ bạn thích làm gì?

lines.t: Mostly playing outside with the other kids in our alley. We’d invent games with nothing but chalk and a ball, and nobody checked on us until dinner time. That kind of unstructured play seems rarer now.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu là chơi ngoài trời với bọn trẻ trong ngõ. Chúng tôi bày trò chỉ với phấn và một quả bóng, và chẳng ai kiểm tra cho đến giờ ăn tối. Kiểu vui chơi tự do đó giờ có vẻ hiếm hơn.

lines.t: Did you have a phone when you were young?
lines.vi: Hồi nhỏ bạn có điện thoại không?

lines.t: Not until I was fifteen, and it could only make calls and send texts. I sometimes think I was lucky — I must have spent thousands more hours reading than children do today.
lines.vi: Mãi đến mười lăm tuổi, và nó chỉ gọi và nhắn tin được. Đôi khi tôi nghĩ mình may mắn — chắc tôi đã dành nhiều hơn hàng nghìn giờ để đọc sách so với trẻ bây giờ.

lines.t: Is your childhood very different from children’s lives now?
lines.vi: Tuổi thơ của bạn có khác nhiều so với trẻ bây giờ không?

lines.t: In some ways. Kids now have more opportunities, like coding classes, but they also seem to have much less freedom to just wander around on their own.
lines.vi: Ở một số mặt. Trẻ giờ có nhiều cơ hội hơn như lớp lập trình, nhưng có vẻ ít tự do lang thang một mình hơn nhiều.

sents.t: Several large studies have found that children who use screens in the hour before bed fall asleep later and sleep less overall.
sents.vi: Nhiều nghiên cứu lớn cho thấy trẻ dùng màn hình trong một giờ trước khi ngủ thì ngủ muộn hơn và ngủ ít hơn tổng thể.

sents.t: Researchers originally blamed the blue light from screens, which can delay the release of the sleep hormone melatonin.
sents.vi: Ban đầu các nhà nghiên cứu đổ lỗi cho ánh sáng xanh từ màn hình, thứ có thể làm chậm việc tiết hormone ngủ melatonin.

sents.t: More recent work suggests that the content matters even more: exciting games and social media keep the brain alert.
sents.vi: Nghiên cứu gần đây cho thấy nội dung còn quan trọng hơn: game hấp dẫn và mạng xã hội giữ não tỉnh táo.

sents.t: Reading an e-book on a dim screen appears to have only a small effect.
sents.vi: Đọc sách điện tử trên màn hình tối dường như chỉ có ảnh hưởng nhỏ.

sents.t: Experts therefore recommend keeping phones out of bedrooms rather than simply using night-mode settings.
sents.vi: Vì vậy chuyên gia khuyên để điện thoại ngoài phòng ngủ thay vì chỉ dùng chế độ ban đêm.

q.q: Recent research suggests that screen content matters more than blue light.
Reading an e-book before bed has a major effect on sleep.
Children who use screens at night have lower exam results.

gram.title: Modal perfects for past speculation and criticism
gram.rule: must have / can’t have + past participle (deduction) · might / could have (possibility) · should / shouldn’t have (criticism, regret)
gram.note: Modal perfects let you speculate about the past and evaluate past decisions — both common in Part 2 and Part 3. Must have = I’m almost sure it happened. Can’t have = I’m almost sure it didn’t. Should have = it was the right thing but didn’t happen. Note: could have also means a possibility that did not happen.

ex.t: Our parents must have worried about different things.
ex.vi: Bố mẹ chúng ta hẳn đã lo về những chuyện khác.

ex.t: He can’t have slept much — he was gaming all night.
ex.vi: Cậu ấy không thể ngủ được nhiều — cậu ấy chơi game cả đêm.

ex.t: I should have spent less time online as a teenager.
ex.vi: Lẽ ra hồi thiếu niên tôi nên dành ít thời gian trên mạng hơn.

ex.t: The school could have done more to stop the bullying.
ex.vi: Nhà trường lẽ ra có thể làm nhiều hơn để ngăn bắt nạt.

drill.t: She ___ been tired; she yawned all day.
drill.vi: Cô ấy hẳn đã mệt; cô ấy ngáp cả ngày.

drill.t: They ___ seen the message — their phone was off.
drill.vi: Họ không thể đã thấy tin nhắn — điện thoại tắt.

drill.t: I ___ listened to my parents.
drill.vi: Lẽ ra tôi nên nghe lời bố mẹ.

drill.t: The accident ___ been much worse.
drill.vi: Tai nạn lẽ ra có thể tệ hơn nhiều.

lines.t: Should young children be allowed to use smartphones?
lines.vi: Có nên cho trẻ nhỏ dùng điện thoại thông minh?

lines.t: In moderation and with clear boundaries, I think it’s unavoidable. Banning phones completely can leave a child socially isolated if all their friends communicate through them. What does matter is what they use them for and that phones stay out of the bedroom at night.
lines.vi: Có chừng mực và giới hạn rõ ràng thì tôi nghĩ là không tránh được. Cấm hẳn điện thoại có thể khiến trẻ bị cô lập nếu mọi bạn bè đều liên lạc qua đó. Điều thực sự quan trọng là chúng dùng để làm gì và điện thoại phải ở ngoài phòng ngủ ban đêm.

lines.t: Are parents today too protective?
lines.vi: Cha mẹ ngày nay có bảo bọc quá mức không?

lines.t: Many are, though it’s understandable given traffic and media stories. The problem is that children who never face small risks — climbing a tree, taking a bus alone — don’t develop resilience, and then the first real failure at university hits them very hard.
lines.vi: Nhiều người như vậy, dù điều đó dễ hiểu khi nghĩ đến giao thông và tin tức. Vấn đề là trẻ chưa bao giờ đối mặt rủi ro nhỏ — trèo cây, tự đi xe buýt — sẽ không phát triển sức bật, rồi thất bại thật sự đầu tiên ở đại học sẽ đánh gục chúng.

lines.t: Who has more influence on children: parents or friends?
lines.vi: Ai ảnh hưởng đến trẻ nhiều hơn: cha mẹ hay bạn bè?

lines.t: It changes with age. Parents dominate in early childhood, but in the teenage years peer influence becomes enormous, especially on things like fashion and slang. Values, though — honesty, how to treat people — seem to come mostly from home.
lines.vi: Nó thay đổi theo tuổi. Cha mẹ chiếm ưu thế khi trẻ còn nhỏ, nhưng tuổi thiếu niên thì ảnh hưởng của bạn bè trở nên rất lớn, nhất là về thời trang và tiếng lóng. Tuy vậy, các giá trị — trung thực, cách đối xử với người khác — có vẻ chủ yếu đến từ gia đình.

gram2.title: Adding emphasis
gram2.rule: do / does / did + verb (I do think …) · What + clause + is … · adverbs: genuinely, undoubtedly, by far, far + comparative · the very + noun
gram2.note: Emphasis makes spoken answers sound natural and engaged, and helps you contrast your view with another: I do understand why parents worry, but … Use far / by far to strengthen comparisons: by far the biggest problem, far more important. Don’t emphasise everything, or nothing stands out.

ex.t: I do think children need some freedom.
ex.vi: Tôi thực sự nghĩ trẻ cần một chút tự do.

ex.t: What worries me most is the effect on sleep.
ex.vi: Điều khiến tôi lo nhất là ảnh hưởng đến giấc ngủ.

ex.t: Outdoor play is far more valuable than many parents realise.
ex.vi: Chơi ngoài trời giá trị hơn nhiều so với nhiều phụ huynh nghĩ.

ex.t: That was by far the hardest year of my childhood.
ex.vi: Đó là năm khó khăn nhất tuổi thơ tôi.

drill.t: I ___ understand your point, but I disagree.
drill.vi: Tôi thực sự hiểu ý bạn, nhưng tôi không đồng ý.

drill.t: Sleep is ___ more important than homework.
drill.vi: Giấc ngủ quan trọng hơn bài tập nhiều.

drill.t: It was by ___ the best holiday.
drill.vi: Đó là kỳ nghỉ tuyệt nhất.

drill.t: She ___ call me last night, actually.
drill.vi: Thực ra tối qua cô ấy có gọi tôi.

cue.card: Describe a childhood memory that is important to you.
points: and explain why this memory is important to you
model: The memory I’d like to describe is the first time I travelled somewhere on my own. I was eleven, and my parents allowed me to take the coach from our town to my grandparents’ village, about two hours away, during the summer holidays.

My mother put me on the coach, gave the driver my grandfather’s phone number and a small bag of food, and that was it. I remember being terrified for the first twenty minutes and then gradually starting to enjoy it — looking out at the rice fields and chatting with an old woman who was taking chickens to market. My grandfather was waiting at the roadside when I arrived, and he pretended not to have been worried, although my grandmother told me later that he must have checked the time every five minutes.

It’s important to me because it was the first time I felt trusted. Looking back, my parents could easily have decided I was too young, and I do think many parents today would. But that small journey gave me a confidence that I still draw on when I face something new. Now that I have a nephew, it makes me think carefully about the balance between keeping children safe and letting them grow.

write.prompt: Some people think that parents should strictly limit the time their children spend using electronic devices. Others think children should be free to use them. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views + position (limits, but adjusted by age, with focus on content and teaching self-control)
Body 1: case for strict limits — sleep, physical activity, attention, addictive design; evidence
Body 2: case for freedom — digital skills, social life, learning resources, self-regulation
Conclusion: guided, age-appropriate limits rather than either extreme
model: Parents today disagree about how much access their children should have to phones, tablets and computers. While some favour strict time limits, others believe children should be allowed to use these devices freely. In my view, clear limits are necessary, particularly for younger children, but they should gradually give way to teaching self-control rather than simply imposing rules.

Those who support strict limits point to evidence about children’s health. Studies have consistently linked heavy screen use, especially at night, to shorter and poorer-quality sleep, which in turn affects concentration at school. Time spent on devices is also often time not spent on physical activity, contributing to a sedentary lifestyle. Furthermore, many apps and games are deliberately designed to be addictive, using rewards and endless feeds that even adults find difficult to resist, so it seems unreasonable to expect a ten-year-old to regulate their own use.

On the other hand, there are good reasons not to be too restrictive. Digital skills are essential for almost every future job, and children who are kept away from technology may fall behind their peers. Devices also give access to an enormous range of educational resources, from language apps to science videos, and for teenagers they are a central part of social life, so a complete ban can leave a child isolated. Perhaps most importantly, if young people never learn to manage their own screen time, they may struggle when they leave home and the rules disappear.

In conclusion, while unrestricted access carries real risks to children’s sleep, health and concentration, rigid limits are not a long-term solution. I believe the best approach is age-appropriate boundaries — strict for young children and more flexible for teenagers — combined with conversations about content and self-discipline, so that children eventually learn to set limits for themselves.

units.title: Space exploration
units.goal: Debate the value of space programmes, using formal linking and inversion for emphasis.

words.ex: Space exploration costs billions every year.
words.exVi: Khám phá vũ trụ tốn hàng tỉ mỗi năm.

words.ex: Satellites help farmers monitor crops.
words.exVi: Vệ tinh giúp nông dân theo dõi mùa màng.

words.vi: quỹ đạo; bay quanh quỹ đạo
words.ex: The station orbits Earth every 90 minutes.
words.exVi: Trạm bay quanh Trái Đất mỗi 90 phút.

words.ex: She was the first astronaut from her country.
words.exVi: Cô ấy là phi hành gia đầu tiên của nước mình.

words.ex: The rocket was launched successfully.
words.exVi: Tên lửa được phóng thành công.

words.ex: Some billionaires dream of colonising Mars.
words.exVi: Một số tỉ phú mơ khai phá sao Hoả.

words.ex: Memory foam was a spin-off from space research.
words.exVi: Mút hoạt tính là sản phẩm phụ từ nghiên cứu vũ trụ.

words.ex: Space debris threatens satellites.
words.exVi: Rác vũ trụ đe doạ các vệ tinh.

words.ex: The privatisation of space has reduced launch costs.
words.exVi: Tư nhân hoá không gian đã giảm chi phí phóng.

words.ex: A probe landed on a comet.
words.exVi: Một tàu thăm dò đã đáp xuống sao chổi.

words.ex: The new telescope can see distant galaxies.
words.exVi: Kính thiên văn mới có thể nhìn thấy thiên hà xa xôi.

words.vi: biện minh, chứng minh là hợp lý
words.ex: Can such costs be justified?
words.exVi: Liệu chi phí như vậy có hợp lý?

words.ex: Climate change is a more pressing concern.
words.exVi: Biến đổi khí hậu là mối lo cấp bách hơn.

words.ex: In the long run, research pays for itself.
words.exVi: Về lâu dài, nghiên cứu sẽ tự hoàn vốn.

words.ex: Satellites improve forecasts, thereby saving lives.
words.exVi: Vệ tinh cải thiện dự báo, nhờ đó cứu người.

words.ex: It is a system whereby countries share data.
words.exVi: Đó là hệ thống theo đó các nước chia sẻ dữ liệu.

words.ex: Launch costs fell, hence the boom in satellites.
words.exVi: Chi phí phóng giảm, do đó bùng nổ vệ tinh.

words.ex: Space research benefits all of humanity.
words.exVi: Nghiên cứu vũ trụ có lợi cho cả nhân loại.

words.vi: biên giới, giới hạn (của hiểu biết)
words.ex: Space is the final frontier.
words.exVi: Vũ trụ là biên giới cuối cùng.

words.ex: The space station is a symbol of international cooperation.
words.exVi: Trạm vũ trụ là biểu tượng của hợp tác quốc tế.

lines.t: Do you like looking at the stars?
lines.vi: Bạn có thích ngắm sao không?

lines.t: I do, but it’s almost impossible in the city because of light pollution. The last time I really saw the Milky Way was on a camping trip in the mountains, and it was breathtaking.
lines.vi: Có, nhưng ở thành phố gần như không thể vì ô nhiễm ánh sáng. Lần cuối tôi thực sự thấy dải Ngân Hà là trong chuyến cắm trại trên núi, và nó đẹp đến nghẹt thở.

lines.t: Were you interested in space as a child?
lines.vi: Hồi nhỏ bạn có quan tâm đến vũ trụ không?

lines.t: Very. I had a poster of the solar system above my bed, and I could name every planet in order, which my parents found slightly strange.
lines.vi: Rất quan tâm. Tôi có tấm áp phích hệ mặt trời phía trên giường và có thể kể tên mọi hành tinh theo thứ tự, điều mà bố mẹ tôi thấy hơi lạ.

lines.t: Would you like to travel into space?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn du hành vào vũ trụ không?

lines.t: Just into orbit, for a few hours, to see Earth from above. But definitely not on a one-way trip to Mars!
lines.vi: Chỉ lên quỹ đạo vài giờ để nhìn Trái Đất từ trên cao. Nhưng chắc chắn không phải chuyến đi một chiều lên sao Hoả!

sents.t: Satellites now provide data for weather forecasts, navigation, banking and disaster response.
sents.vi: Vệ tinh hiện cung cấp dữ liệu cho dự báo thời tiết, định vị, ngân hàng và ứng phó thảm hoạ.

sents.t: Improved typhoon forecasts in Asia have helped governments evacuate millions of people in time.
sents.vi: Dự báo bão tốt hơn ở châu Á đã giúp chính phủ sơ tán hàng triệu người kịp thời.

sents.t: Many everyday products, including scratch-resistant lenses and some medical scanners, grew out of space research.
sents.vi: Nhiều sản phẩm hằng ngày, gồm tròng kính chống xước và một số máy chụp y tế, ra đời từ nghiên cứu vũ trụ.

sents.t: However, some economists argue that the same money spent directly on these technologies would have produced them faster.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, một số nhà kinh tế cho rằng nếu chi trực tiếp cùng số tiền cho các công nghệ này thì chúng đã ra đời nhanh hơn.

sents.t: Meanwhile, the growing amount of space debris threatens the satellites on which these services depend.
sents.vi: Trong khi đó, lượng rác vũ trụ ngày càng tăng đe doạ chính các vệ tinh mà những dịch vụ này phụ thuộc.

q.q: Satellites help with disaster response.
All economists agree that space research is the fastest way to develop new technology.
Space debris has already destroyed several weather satellites.

gram.title: Formal linking: thereby, whereby, hence, thus
gram.rule: …, thereby + -ing (as a result) · a system / process whereby + clause (by which) · hence + noun (that is why) · thus (therefore)
gram.note: These words are typical of academic writing and help you connect ideas precisely. Thereby is followed by -ing and shows a result of the previous action. Whereby means “by which” and describes how a system works. Hence can be followed by a noun alone: Costs have fallen, hence the rapid growth. Use them sparingly.

ex.t: Reusable rockets cut costs, thereby making space more accessible.
ex.vi: Tên lửa tái sử dụng giảm chi phí, nhờ đó giúp không gian dễ tiếp cận hơn.

ex.t: It is an agreement whereby countries share satellite data.
ex.vi: Đó là thoả thuận theo đó các nước chia sẻ dữ liệu vệ tinh.

ex.t: Launch costs have fallen sharply, hence the boom in small satellites.
ex.vi: Chi phí phóng giảm mạnh, vì thế mới bùng nổ vệ tinh nhỏ.

ex.t: The data were incomplete; thus, no conclusion could be drawn.
ex.vi: Dữ liệu chưa đầy đủ; do đó không thể kết luận.

drill.t: The project reduced pollution, thereby ___ public health.
drill.vi: Dự án giảm ô nhiễm, nhờ đó cải thiện sức khoẻ cộng đồng.

drill.t: A scheme ___ students can study abroad.
drill.vi: Một chương trình theo đó sinh viên có thể du học.

drill.t: Prices fell, ___ the increase in demand.
drill.vi: Giá giảm, do đó nhu cầu tăng.

drill.t: The test failed; ___, the launch was delayed.
drill.vi: Thử nghiệm thất bại; do đó việc phóng bị hoãn.

lines.t: Is space exploration a waste of money?
lines.vi: Khám phá vũ trụ có phải lãng phí tiền không?

lines.t: I don’t think so, although it’s a fair question when people lack clean water. What people often forget is that most space spending goes on satellites that we use every day for weather, navigation and communication. Not only does that infrastructure save lives, but it also supports entire industries.
lines.vi: Tôi không nghĩ vậy, dù đó là câu hỏi hợp lý khi nhiều người còn thiếu nước sạch. Điều người ta hay quên là phần lớn chi tiêu vũ trụ dành cho vệ tinh mà ta dùng hằng ngày cho thời tiết, định vị và liên lạc. Hạ tầng đó không chỉ cứu người mà còn nuôi sống cả những ngành công nghiệp.

lines.t: Should private companies be allowed to explore space?
lines.vi: Có nên cho công ty tư nhân khám phá vũ trụ?

lines.t: They’ve already made launches dramatically cheaper, hence the huge growth in satellites. But space is shared by everyone, so there need to be international rules — on debris, for example — otherwise a few companies could damage orbits that all countries depend on.
lines.vi: Họ đã làm việc phóng rẻ đi rất nhiều, vì thế vệ tinh mới tăng mạnh như vậy. Nhưng không gian là của chung, nên cần quy tắc quốc tế — ví dụ về rác vũ trụ — nếu không vài công ty có thể làm hỏng những quỹ đạo mà mọi quốc gia phụ thuộc.

lines.t: Will humans ever live on other planets?
lines.vi: Con người có bao giờ sống trên hành tinh khác không?

lines.t: Perhaps small research bases, like those in Antarctica, within this century. But colonising Mars on a large scale seems far less realistic than people suggest. Never before have we faced such a hostile environment, and frankly it would be far easier to look after the planet we already have.
lines.vi: Có lẽ là những trạm nghiên cứu nhỏ như ở Nam Cực, trong thế kỷ này. Nhưng khai phá sao Hoả quy mô lớn có vẻ kém thực tế hơn nhiều so với lời người ta nói. Chưa bao giờ chúng ta đối mặt môi trường khắc nghiệt đến thế, và thật lòng chăm sóc hành tinh mình đang có dễ hơn nhiều.

gram2.title: Inversion for emphasis
gram2.rule: Not only + auxiliary + subject …, but … also · Never before + auxiliary + subject … · Rarely / Seldom + auxiliary + subject … · Only by + -ing + auxiliary + subject …
gram2.note: Inversion puts a negative or limiting expression first and then reverses the subject and auxiliary, as in a question. It sounds formal and emphatic, so it suits Task 2 conclusions and the occasional Part 3 answer. Use it once per essay at most; overuse sounds unnatural.

ex.t: Not only does space research create jobs, but it also drives innovation.
ex.vi: Nghiên cứu vũ trụ không chỉ tạo việc làm mà còn thúc đẩy đổi mới.

ex.t: Never before has space been so accessible to private companies.
ex.vi: Chưa bao giờ không gian dễ tiếp cận với công ty tư nhân như vậy.

ex.t: Rarely do people consider how much they rely on satellites.
ex.vi: Hiếm khi người ta nghĩ mình phụ thuộc vào vệ tinh nhiều thế nào.

ex.t: Only by cooperating can countries manage space debris.
ex.vi: Chỉ bằng cách hợp tác các nước mới quản lý được rác vũ trụ.

drill.t: Not only ___ expensive, but it is also risky.
drill.vi: Nó không chỉ đắt mà còn rủi ro.

drill.t: Never before ___ so many satellites in orbit.
drill.vi: Chưa bao giờ có nhiều vệ tinh trên quỹ đạo đến vậy.

drill.t: Rarely ___ such a clear night.
drill.vi: Hiếm khi ta thấy đêm quang đãng như vậy.

drill.t: Only by working together ___ succeed.
drill.vi: Chỉ bằng cách làm việc cùng nhau ta mới thành công.

cue.card: Describe a science topic that you would like to learn more about.
points: how you first became interested in it
what you already know about it
and explain why you want to learn more about it
model: The topic I’d love to understand better is how astronomers detect planets around other stars — what are called exoplanets.

I first became interested about five years ago when I read a news article saying that scientists had found seven Earth-sized planets orbiting a star called TRAPPIST-1, about forty light years away. What amazed me was that nobody had actually seen these planets; they were detected because the star’s light dimmed very slightly every time a planet passed in front of it.

What I know so far is fairly basic. There are a couple of main methods — measuring that tiny drop in light, or measuring how a star wobbles because of a planet’s gravity — and thousands of exoplanets have now been confirmed. Some are in what’s called the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. I want to learn more because it touches on probably the biggest question there is: whether we’re alone. Rarely does a scientific field move this fast, either — new telescopes are producing discoveries every month — so I’d like to understand the methods properly instead of just reading headlines.

write.prompt: Some people think that the money spent on space exploration would be better used to solve problems on Earth. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + position (disagree: space spending is small and often solves Earth problems)
Body 1: concede — urgent needs, opportunity cost, prestige projects
Body 2: main argument — satellites for climate, agriculture, disasters; spin-offs; scale of budgets
Conclusion: restate + recommendation (prioritise Earth-observation and cooperation over prestige missions)
model: It is sometimes argued that funds devoted to exploring space should instead be spent on pressing problems on our own planet, such as poverty and disease. Although I understand this view, I largely disagree with it, since space programmes cost far less than is commonly assumed and frequently contribute to solving the very problems their critics mention.

Admittedly, the argument has some force. Hundreds of millions of people still lack clean water or basic healthcare, and it can seem morally questionable to spend billions on sending robots to Mars while these needs remain unmet. Moreover, some space missions are driven more by national prestige than by scientific value, and the resources involved, in terms of both money and highly skilled engineers, could undoubtedly achieve a great deal if redirected towards health or renewable energy.

Nevertheless, this view overlooks how much of space spending directly benefits life on Earth. Satellites monitor deforestation, measure rising sea levels and track crop health, thereby providing data that is essential for tackling climate change and food insecurity. Improved forecasts of typhoons and floods, made possible by weather satellites, have allowed governments to evacuate millions of people in time. In addition, research for space missions has produced numerous practical spin-offs, from water purification systems to medical imaging technologies. It is also worth noting that space agencies typically receive less than half of one per cent of national budgets, so cancelling them would make little difference to the scale of global problems.

In conclusion, while the needs on Earth are undeniably urgent, I do not accept that space exploration is a misuse of money. Not only does it cost relatively little, but it also provides tools that are vital for addressing environmental and humanitarian challenges. Governments should, however, prioritise missions with clear practical benefits over those designed mainly to enhance national prestige.

levels.name: Band 7→7.5
levels.title: Advanced: precision, nuance and argument
levels.desc: Bioethics, inequality, migration, university funding, public health, climate policy, heritage, fashion, leadership and volunteering — issues where examiners reward precise vocabulary and fully developed arguments.
goals: Choose precise collocations rather than general words (e.g. “bear the brunt”, “a disproportionate share”)
Present a counter-argument and rebut it convincingly
Use a wide range of structures — conditionals without if, causatives, prepositional relatives — with very few errors
Speak in Part 3 with speculation, evaluation and abstract examples, not only personal ones
Write Task 1 overviews that compare trends across categories, not just within them
extra: One full Cambridge practice test (all four skills) every week under exam conditions
Read one long-form academic article a week (The Economist, Aeon, Scientific American) and summarise it in 150 words
Record a 3-part Speaking mock each week and transcribe two minutes to find your error patterns
Get every Writing task marked by a qualified teacher, focusing on Lexical Resource and Task Response

units.title: Genetic engineering & bioethics
units.goal: Debate the ethics of genetic science, using conditionals without if and evidence-based hedging.

words.ex: Editing human embryos is banned in many countries.
words.exVi: Chỉnh sửa phôi người bị cấm ở nhiều nước.

words.exVi: Nghiên cứu thiếu sự giám sát phù hợp.
